P.title: P.blurb
Space: Planets, stars, galaxies and the search for life.

P.title: sp-solar.summary
Space: A tour of our neighbourhood, from the Sun to the edge.

P.title: sp-solar.q0.x
Space: Its thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat.

P.title: sp-solar.q1.q
Space: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?

P.title: sp-solar.q1.x
Space: The Sun is 150 million km away.

P.title: sp-solar.c0.text
Space: The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the Solar System. It's a ball of hot plasma, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core at about 15 million °C.

P.title: sp-solar.c1.text
Space: Four small rocky planets sit close to the Sun; four giants lie further out. A memory trick: "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming".

P.title: sp-solar.c2.text
Space: The inner planets are made of rock and metal. The outer ones are gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) and ice giants (Uranus, Neptune), with no solid surface to stand on.

P.title: sp-solar.c3.text
Space: Venus is further from the Sun than Mercury but hotter, about 465 °C, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect.

P.title: sp-solar.c4.text
Space: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth that has lasted for centuries.

P.title: sp-solar.c5.text
Space: Saturn's rings are made of countless chunks of ice and rock, from dust to house-sized. They're about 280,000 km wide but in places only about 10 metres thick.

P.title: sp-solar.c6.text
Space: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet as a body that has cleared its orbit. Pluto shares its zone with many icy objects, so it became a dwarf planet.

P.title: sp-solar.c7.text
Space: Asteroids are rocky leftovers, mostly between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy bodies from the outer Solar System that grow glowing tails when they near the Sun.

P.title: sp-solar.c8.text
Space: Astronomers measure the Solar System in astronomical units: 1 AU is the Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us.

P.title: sp-solar.c9.title
Space: A model in a football stadium

P.title: sp-solar.c9.text
Space: Shrink the Sun to a football in the centre circle. Earth is a peppercorn about 25 m away, Jupiter a marble about 130 m away, and Neptune a small bead about 715 m away.

P.title: sp-stars.summary
Space: How stars live and die, and where we are in the universe.

P.title: sp-stars.q1.q
Space: Which colour stars are the hottest?

P.title: sp-stars.q2.q
Space: What will the Sun become at the end of its life?

P.title: sp-stars.q2.x
Space: It's not massive enough to explode.

P.title: sp-stars.c0.text
Space: Stars form inside giant clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls a clump together until the core is hot and dense enough to fuse hydrogen, and a star lights up.

P.title: sp-stars.c1.text
Space: Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium. A little mass is turned into a lot of energy, following Einstein's E = mc².

P.title: sp-stars.c2.text
Space: A star's colour shows its temperature: red stars are the coolest, blue the hottest. Our Sun is a yellowish-white star in the middle.

P.title: sp-stars.c3.title
Space: Life of a star like the Sun

P.title: sp-stars.c3.text
Space: The Sun is about halfway through a 10-billion-year life. In about 5 billion years it will swell into a red giant, then shed its outer layers and leave a small white dwarf.

P.title: sp-stars.c4.text
Space: Stars much heavier than the Sun end in a supernova explosion that can briefly outshine a galaxy. The core becomes a neutron star or, if heavy enough, a black hole.

P.title: sp-stars.c5.text
Space: Most of the atoms in your body, like carbon, oxygen and iron, were made inside stars that exploded before the Sun was born.

P.title: sp-stars.c6.text
Space: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope took the first image of one, in the galaxy M87.

P.title: sp-stars.c7.text
Space: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year: about 9.5 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

P.title: sp-stars.c8.text
Space: Our galaxy is a barred spiral of 100–400 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. The Sun sits in a quiet arm about 26,000 light-years from the centre.

P.title: sp-stars.c9.text
Space: The observable universe holds perhaps 100 billion to 2 trillion galaxies. The Andromeda galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away, is the furthest thing you can see with the naked eye.

P.title: sp-explore.q0.q
Space: Who was the first human in space?

P.title: sp-explore.q1.q
Space: Why can rockets work in space without air?

P.title: sp-explore.c0.text
Space: After the Second World War, the USA and the Soviet Union competed to reach space first. The Soviets launched the first satellite and the first human; the Americans landed on the Moon.

P.title: sp-explore.c1.text
Space: Rockets push hot gas out of the back at high speed; by Newton's third law, the gas pushes the rocket forward. They work in a vacuum because they carry their own oxygen.

P.title: sp-explore.c1.viz.steps.1
Space: Hot gas rushes out the back

P.title: sp-explore.c2.text
Space: To orbit, you need to go sideways fast enough to keep "falling" around the Earth without hitting it: about 7.8 km/s, or 28,000 km/h, in low orbit.

P.title: sp-explore.c3.text
Space: On 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Twelve people walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.

P.title: sp-explore.c4.text
Space: The ISS has been continuously crewed since November 2000. It's about the size of a football pitch and circles the Earth about 16 times a day.

P.title: sp-explore.c5.text
Space: Above the atmosphere, telescopes see more clearly. Hubble (1990) transformed astronomy; James Webb (2021) sees infrared light from the first galaxies.

P.title: sp-explore.c6.text
Space: Rovers have explored Mars since 1997. Perseverance, landed in 2021, collects rock samples and carried Ingenuity, the first helicopter to fly on another planet.

P.title: sp-explore.c7.text
Space: Since 2015, rockets have landed their boosters back on Earth to fly again. Reuse has cut the cost of reaching orbit and made launches routine.

P.title: sp-explore.c8.text
Space: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object, more than 24 billion km away. It carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.

P.title: sp-explore.c9.text
Space: Thousands of satellites support daily life: GPS navigation, weather forecasts, TV, internet and monitoring of fires and crops.

P.title: sp-moon.q0.x
Space: The tilt changes the angle of sunlight.

P.title: sp-moon.q1.q
Space: Why does the Moon look red in a lunar eclipse?

P.title: sp-moon.q1.o1
Space: Earth's atmosphere bends red light onto it

P.title: sp-moon.q1.x
Space: Like all the sunsets on Earth at once.

P.title: sp-moon.c0.text
Space: Seasons aren't caused by distance from the Sun. Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so each hemisphere takes turns leaning towards the Sun and getting more direct light.

P.title: sp-moon.c0.viz.items.0.w
Space: Closer to the Sun in summer

P.title: sp-moon.c0.viz.items.0.r
Space: Earth's tilt changes the angle of sunlight

P.title: sp-moon.c1.text
Space: Earth spins on its axis once about every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the other side has night. The Sun "rises" because we turn towards it.

P.title: sp-moon.c2.text
Space: The Moon doesn't make light; it reflects sunlight. As it orbits Earth every 29.5 days, we see different amounts of its lit half.

P.title: sp-moon.c3.text
Space: The Moon always shows us the same face because it spins exactly once per orbit, known as tidal locking. The far side isn't dark; it gets as much sunlight as the near side.

P.title: sp-moon.c3.viz.items.0.w
Space: The dark side of the Moon

P.title: sp-moon.c3.viz.items.0.r
Space: the far side, which gets sunlight too

P.title: sp-moon.c4.text
Space: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth. By coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times further away, so they look the same size.

P.title: sp-moon.c5.text
Space: In a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. The Moon turns coppery red because Earth's atmosphere bends red sunlight onto it.

P.title: sp-moon.c6.text
Space: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, creating two bulges of water: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. As Earth turns, most coasts get two high tides a day.

P.title: sp-moon.c7.text
Space: The leading theory: about 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body called Theia crashed into the young Earth, and the debris came together to form the Moon.

P.title: sp-moon.c8.text
Space: Meteors are specks of dust burning up in the atmosphere at tens of km per second. Meteor showers like the Perseids (August) happen when Earth crosses a comet's trail.

P.title: sp-moon.c9.text
Space: Planets don't twinkle as much as stars and move slowly against the background over weeks. Venus is often the brightest "star" right after sunset or before dawn.

P.title: sp-moon.c9.viz.items.3
Space: Jupiter: bright all night when visible

P.title: sp-life.summary
Space: Exoplanets, aliens and the big questions.

P.title: sp-life.q0.o1
Space: A star dims as a planet passes

P.title: sp-life.q1.q
Space: Which moon sprays water from a hidden ocean?

P.title: sp-life.c0.text
Space: An exoplanet orbits a star other than the Sun. The first around a Sun-like star was found in 1995; today more than 5,000 are confirmed.

P.title: sp-life.c1.text
Space: Most exoplanets are found by the transit method: when a planet passes in front of its star, the star dims slightly and regularly.

P.title: sp-life.c1.viz.steps.2
Space: A planet is passing in front

P.title: sp-life.c2.text
Space: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where it's neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water on a planet's surface.

P.title: sp-life.c3.text
Space: Life as we know it needs liquid water, an energy source and chemistry built around carbon. On Earth, microbes live in boiling springs, ice and deep rock.

P.title: sp-life.c4.text
Space: Mars may once have had rivers; Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's moon Enceladus have oceans under their ice, and Enceladus sprays water into space.

P.title: sp-life.c5.text
Space: In 1961 Frank Drake listed the factors needed to estimate how many civilisations might be signalling in our galaxy. Most of the numbers are still unknown.

P.title: sp-life.c5.viz.f
Space: N = R* · fp · ne · fl · fi · fc · L

P.title: sp-life.c6.text
Space: If the galaxy is old and huge, why haven't we met anyone? Possible answers: life is rare, civilisations don't last, distances are too vast, or we're not looking the right way.

P.title: sp-life.c7.text
Space: The Search for Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence listens for radio signals from other civilisations. The famous 1977 "Wow! signal" was never detected again.

P.title: sp-life.c8.text
Space: In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a message towards a star cluster 25,000 light-years away. The Voyager golden records carry greetings in 55 languages.

P.title: sp-life.c9.text
Space: In 1990, Voyager 1 photographed Earth from about 6 billion km away: a speck of light less than a pixel wide. Carl Sagan used it to remind us how small and precious our world is.

P.title: sp-mars.q1.q
Space: How long is a Martian day?

P.title: sp-mars.q2.o1
Space: The tallest volcano in the Solar System

P.title: sp-mars.c0.text
Space: Mars is red because its dust is rich in iron oxide: rust. The fine dust gets everywhere, even tinting the sky a butterscotch colour.

P.title: sp-mars.c1.text
Space: Mars is about half Earth's width with roughly a third of its gravity. The average temperature is around −65 °C, and the air is 100 times thinner than ours.

P.title: sp-mars.c2.text
Space: A Martian day, called a sol, lasts 24 h 37 min, very close to ours. A Martian year is 687 Earth days, so its seasons last about twice as long.

P.title: sp-mars.c3.text
Space: Mars has the tallest volcano in the Solar System: Olympus Mons, about 22 km high, two and a half times the height of Everest, and about 600 km wide, roughly the length of Portugal.

P.title: sp-mars.c4.text
Space: A canyon system about 4,000 km long and up to 7 km deep cuts across Mars. On Earth it would stretch roughly from Lisbon to Moscow.

P.title: sp-mars.c5.text
Space: Dry riverbeds, deltas and minerals that form in water show Mars once had lakes and rivers. Today water survives as ice at the poles and underground.

P.title: sp-mars.c6.text
Space: Mars has two small, lumpy moons, Phobos and Deimos, probably captured asteroids or debris from an impact. Phobos is slowly spiralling inwards.

P.title: sp-mars.c7.text
Space: Mars has dust storms that can cover the whole planet for weeks. A 2018 storm ended the Opportunity rover's mission by blocking sunlight to its solar panels.

P.title: sp-mars.c8.text
Space: Launch windows to Mars open about every 26 months, when the planets line up. The trip takes six to nine months.

P.title: sp-mars.c9.text
Space: Humans on Mars would need shelter from radiation and cold, oxygen made from CO₂, and water dug from ice. It's possible, but far harder than living in Antarctica.

P.title: sp-giants.summary
Space: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and their worlds.

P.title: sp-giants.q0.q
Space: Which moon is the largest in the Solar System?

P.title: sp-giants.c0.text
Space: Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune have more water, ammonia and methane "ices", which is why they're called ice giants.

P.title: sp-giants.c1.text
Space: Jupiter's huge gravity flings or captures many comets and asteroids. It may shield the inner planets, though it can also send some our way.

P.title: sp-giants.c2.text
Space: Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanic place known, with hundreds of volcanoes. Jupiter's gravity squeezes it like a stress ball, heating its interior.

P.title: sp-giants.c3.text
Space: Under Europa's icy crust lies a salty ocean with perhaps twice the water of all Earth's oceans. NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will study it.

P.title: sp-giants.c4.text
Space: Ganymede, another moon of Jupiter, is the largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than the planet Mercury, and has its own magnetic field.

P.title: sp-giants.c5.text
Space: Saturn's moon Titan has a thick orange atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. The Huygens probe landed there in 2005.

P.title: sp-giants.c6.text
Space: Saturn's average density is lower than water's. Given a big enough bathtub, it would float, although it's a ball of gas, not a solid.

P.title: sp-giants.c7.text
Space: Uranus is tilted about 98°, so it rolls around the Sun on its side. Each pole gets 42 years of continuous daylight and then 42 years of night.

P.title: sp-giants.c8.text
Space: Neptune, the farthest planet, has the fastest winds in the Solar System, above 2,000 km/h. It was found in 1846 by mathematics before anyone saw it.

P.title: sp-giants.c9.text
Space: Only Voyager 2 has visited Uranus and Neptune, in 1986 and 1989. Galileo and Juno studied Jupiter; Cassini orbited Saturn for 13 years.

P.title: sp-sun.q1.o1
Space: Solar particles hitting the upper atmosphere

P.title: sp-sun.c0.text
Space: Energy is made in the core, then crawls outwards through the radiative zone over tens of thousands of years, bubbles up through the convective zone and escapes from the surface.

P.title: sp-sun.c1.text
Space: The surface is about 5,500 °C, but the outer atmosphere, the corona, reaches over a million degrees. Why it's so hot is still being studied.

P.title: sp-sun.c2.text
Space: Sunspots are cooler, darker patches where magnetic fields block heat. Their numbers rise and fall over an 11-year solar cycle.

P.title: sp-sun.c3.text
Space: Flares are sudden bursts of energy from tangled magnetic fields. Big ones can disrupt radio, GPS and satellites on Earth.

P.title: sp-sun.c4.text
Space: The Sun constantly blows charged particles into space at around 400 km/s. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of them.

P.title: sp-sun.c5.text
Space: When solar particles hit the upper atmosphere near the poles, oxygen glows green and red, and nitrogen glows blue and purple: the northern and southern lights.

P.title: sp-sun.c6.text
Space: In 1859 a huge solar storm made auroras visible near the tropics and gave telegraph operators electric shocks. A similar storm today could damage power grids.

P.title: sp-sun.c7.text
Space: Spacecraft watch the Sun to warn of storms a day or more ahead, so satellite and grid operators can prepare.

P.title: sp-sun.c8.text
Space: Looking at the Sun, even briefly during a partial eclipse, can permanently damage your retina. Use certified eclipse glasses or project the image.

P.title: sp-sun.c9.text
Space: Launched in 2018, NASA's Parker Solar Probe has flown through the corona and is the fastest human-made object, reaching about 690,000 km/h.

P.title: sp-bigbang.summary
Space: How the universe began and grew.

P.title: sp-bigbang.q0.x
Space: Measured from the expansion and afterglow.

P.title: sp-bigbang.q1.o1
Space: Galaxies are moving away from us

P.title: sp-bigbang.c0.text
Space: In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther they are, the faster. Space itself is expanding.

P.title: sp-bigbang.c1.text
Space: If everything is moving apart, it was once closer together. Run the film back about 13.8 billion years and everything was extremely hot and dense: the Big Bang.

P.title: sp-bigbang.c2.text
Space: The Big Bang wasn't a bomb going off in empty space. It was the rapid expansion of space itself, everywhere at once.

P.title: sp-bigbang.c3.text
Space: Imagine raisins in rising dough: every raisin sees all the others moving away, and the farthest move fastest. There's no centre.

P.title: sp-bigbang.c4.text
Space: Within the first three minutes, the universe cooled enough for protons and neutrons to form hydrogen and helium nuclei. Heavier elements came much later, from stars.

P.title: sp-bigbang.c5.text
Space: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe became transparent. That light still fills space as faint microwaves, found by accident in 1965.

P.title: sp-bigbang.c6.text
Space: Light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths, like a siren dropping in pitch as it drives away.

P.title: sp-bigbang.c7.text
Space: We can only see as far as light has had time to reach us. Because space expanded meanwhile, the edge of what we see is about 46 billion light-years away.

P.title: sp-bigbang.c8.text
Space: Fred Hoyle, who preferred a "steady state" universe, coined "Big Bang" on BBC radio in 1949. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, first proposed the idea.

P.title: sp-bigbang.c9.text
Space: Most evidence points to a universe expanding forever, getting colder and darker over unimaginable time: the "heat death". Other endings are still debated.

P.title: sp-blackholes.summary
Space: The strangest objects in the universe.

P.title: sp-blackholes.q0.x
Space: Not even light escapes from inside.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c0.text
Space: A black hole's boundary is the event horizon: the point of no return. Inside, the escape speed exceeds the speed of light.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c0.viz.items.1
Space: Event horizon: point of no return

P.title: sp-blackholes.c1.text
Space: Most stellar black holes form when a star more than about 20 times the Sun's mass runs out of fuel and its core collapses.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c2.text
Space: If the Sun became a black hole, its event horizon would be only about 6 km across. Earth's would be the size of a marble.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c3.text
Space: Almost every big galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its centre. Ours, Sagittarius A*, is about 4 million times the Sun's mass.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c4.text
Space: Near a small black hole, gravity pulls far harder on your feet than your head, stretching you like spaghetti.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c5.text
Space: Near a black hole, time runs slower compared with far away. To a distant observer, something falling in seems to freeze at the edge.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c6.text
Space: Black holes are found by their effects: stars orbiting something invisible, glowing hot gas swirling around them and ripples in spacetime.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c7.text
Space: In 2015 the LIGO detectors caught ripples in spacetime from two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away, as Einstein had predicted a century earlier.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c8.text
Space: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, linking radio dishes across the world into an Earth-sized telescope, imaged the shadow of M87's black hole. Sagittarius A* followed in 2022.

P.title: sp-blackholes.c9.text
Space: Stephen Hawking calculated in 1974 that black holes should slowly leak energy and eventually evaporate, though for real ones this takes far longer than the universe's age.

P.title: sp-telescopes.summary
Space: How we see the invisible universe.

P.title: sp-telescopes.q0.q
Space: Why do we see Andromeda as it was 2.5 million years ago?

P.title: sp-telescopes.q0.o1
Space: Its light took that long to reach us

P.title: sp-telescopes.q0.x
Space: Light travels at a finite speed.

P.title: sp-telescopes.q1.q
Space: How do we know what stars are made of?

P.title: sp-telescopes.q2.q
Space: Why does Webb see in infrared?

P.title: sp-telescopes.q2.o1
Space: Light from early galaxies is stretched to infrared

P.title: sp-telescopes.c0.text
Space: Light takes time to travel, so we see the Moon as it was 1.3 seconds ago, the Sun 8 minutes ago and Andromeda 2.5 million years ago.

P.title: sp-telescopes.c1.text
Space: In 1609–10 Galileo pointed a simple telescope at the sky and saw Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus, sunspots and countless stars in the Milky Way.

P.title: sp-telescopes.c2.text
Space: Refracting telescopes use lenses; reflecting telescopes, invented by Newton, use curved mirrors. All big research telescopes are reflectors, because mirrors can be made huge.

P.title: sp-telescopes.c3.text
Space: A telescope's power to collect light depends on its mirror area. The upcoming Extremely Large Telescope in Chile has a 39 m mirror.

P.title: sp-telescopes.c4.text
Space: Visible light is a tiny slice of the spectrum. Different wavelengths reveal different things, from cold dust in radio to exploding stars in X-rays.

P.title: sp-telescopes.c5.text
Space: Infrared light passes through dust clouds and shows cool objects. James Webb sees in infrared to spot newborn stars and the first galaxies, whose light was stretched by expansion.

P.title: sp-telescopes.c6.text
Space: Earth's atmosphere blurs starlight and blocks X-rays, UV and much infrared. Space telescopes avoid both problems.

P.title: sp-telescopes.c7.text
Space: Radio telescopes are giant dishes. Linking dishes across continents creates a virtual telescope as wide as the distance between them.

P.title: sp-telescopes.c8.text
Space: Splitting starlight into a rainbow reveals dark lines: fingerprints of the elements in the star. That's how we know what stars are made of without visiting.

P.title: sp-telescopes.c9.text
Space: Light pollution hides most stars from city dwellers. Portugal's Dark Sky Alqueva reserve was the world's first "Starlight Tourism Destination", certified in 2011.

P.title: sp-gravity.summary
Space: Why things fall, and why the Moon doesn't.

P.title: sp-gravity.q0.q
Space: Why are astronauts on the ISS weightless?

P.title: sp-gravity.q0.o1
Space: They're in free fall with the station

P.title: sp-gravity.q0.x
Space: Gravity is still about 90% as strong.

P.title: sp-gravity.q1.q
Space: Double the distance, and gravity becomes…

P.title: sp-gravity.c0.text
Space: Isaac Newton realised the force that makes an apple fall also keeps the Moon in orbit. Every mass attracts every other mass.

P.title: sp-gravity.c1.text
Space: Double the distance and gravity drops to a quarter. Triple it and it drops to a ninth.

P.title: sp-gravity.c2.text
Space: An orbiting spacecraft is constantly falling towards Earth but moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it. Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain.

P.title: sp-gravity.c2.viz.steps.2
Space: Fast enough: falls around the Earth

P.title: sp-gravity.c3.text
Space: Astronauts on the ISS feel weightless not because there's no gravity, which is about 90% as strong there, but because they're falling together with the station.

P.title: sp-gravity.c3.viz.items.0.r
Space: Gravity is ~90% as strong, they're in free fall

P.title: sp-gravity.c4.text
Space: Your mass stays the same everywhere; your weight depends on gravity. A 70 kg person would weigh about as much as 12 kg on the Moon.

P.title: sp-gravity.c5.text
Space: Johannes Kepler found that planets move in ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times and that farther planets take longer to orbit.

P.title: sp-gravity.c6.text
Space: To escape Earth's gravity completely, you'd need about 11.2 km/s. On the Moon, just 2.4 km/s.

P.title: sp-gravity.c7.text
Space: Spacecraft swing past planets to steal a bit of their orbital speed, like a ball bouncing off a moving train. Voyager used Jupiter and Saturn this way.

P.title: sp-gravity.c8.text
Space: There are five points where a small object can hold position relative to two big bodies. Webb sits at L2, 1.5 million km from Earth, opposite the Sun.

P.title: sp-gravity.c8.viz.items.0.b
Space: between Sun and Earth, solar observatories

P.title: sp-gravity.c9.text
Space: At about 36,000 km up, a satellite orbits once a day, staying over the same spot. TV satellite dishes point at a fixed point in the sky for this reason.

P.title: sp-relativity.q0.q
Space: What happens to a clock moving very fast?

P.title: sp-relativity.q1.o1
Space: Satellite clocks run at a different rate

P.title: sp-relativity.q1.x
Space: Uncorrected, errors grow by km a day.

P.title: sp-relativity.c0.text
Space: Light travels at about 300,000 km per second in a vacuum, and every observer measures the same speed, however fast they move. That simple fact changes everything.

P.title: sp-relativity.c0.viz.items.1.l
Space: laps of Earth in a second

P.title: sp-relativity.c1.text
Space: Moving clocks run slow. An astronaut travelling near light speed would return to find more time had passed on Earth than for them.

P.title: sp-relativity.c2.text
Space: One twin flies to a star at 87% of light speed and back; the other stays home. On return, the traveller has aged about half as much. Time dilation itself has been confirmed with atomic clocks flown on planes.

P.title: sp-relativity.c3.text
Space: Objects moving very fast are shorter in their direction of motion, as measured by someone watching them pass. It's only noticeable near light speed.

P.title: sp-relativity.c4.text
Space: Mass and energy are two forms of the same thing. A tiny amount of mass holds huge energy, which powers the Sun and nuclear reactors.

P.title: sp-relativity.c4.viz.items.2.m
Space: speed of light squared, a huge number

P.title: sp-relativity.c5.text
Space: In general relativity (1915), mass curves spacetime and objects follow the curves. Think of a heavy ball on a trampoline making marbles roll towards it.

P.title: sp-relativity.c6.text
Space: In 1919, Arthur Eddington measured starlight bending around the Sun during an eclipse, exactly as Einstein predicted. It made Einstein world famous.

P.title: sp-relativity.c7.text
Space: GPS satellites' clocks run faster by about 38 microseconds a day because of weaker gravity and slower because of speed. Without corrections, positions would drift by kilometres daily.

P.title: sp-relativity.c8.text
Space: Massive galaxy clusters bend light from galaxies behind them, creating arcs and multiple images. Astronomers use these natural magnifying glasses.

P.title: sp-relativity.c9.text
Space: Nothing with mass can reach light speed: the closer you get, the more energy each extra bit of speed costs. Information can't travel faster than light either.

P.title: sp-astronauts.summary
Space: Eating, sleeping and working in orbit.

P.title: sp-astronauts.q0.q
Space: Why do astronauts eat tortillas instead of bread?

P.title: sp-astronauts.q1.q
Space: Why do astronauts get taller in space?

P.title: sp-astronauts.c0.text
Space: Space agencies pick a handful from thousands of applicants. ESA's 2022 selection drew over 22,500 applications for 17 places, including astronauts and reserves.

P.title: sp-astronauts.c1.text
Space: Astronauts train for years: spacewalks rehearsed underwater, survival training, Russian language, robotics and flights in planes that create short bursts of weightlessness.

P.title: sp-astronauts.c2.text
Space: Food comes in pouches and tins; crumbs are dangerous, so tortillas replace bread. Taste dulls in orbit, so astronauts love spicy sauces.

P.title: sp-astronauts.c3.text
Space: Astronauts sleep in small cabins in sleeping bags tied to the wall. There's no "up", so you can sleep in any orientation.

P.title: sp-astronauts.c3.viz.items.0
Space: Sleeping bag tied to the wall

P.title: sp-astronauts.c4.text
Space: Without gravity, muscles and bones weaken, fluids shift to the head, and the spine stretches; astronauts grow about 3 cm taller temporarily.

P.title: sp-astronauts.c5.text
Space: To fight bone and muscle loss, ISS crews exercise about two hours a day on a treadmill with harnesses, a bike and a resistance machine.

P.title: sp-astronauts.c5.viz.items.2.l
Space: bone lost a month without it

P.title: sp-astronauts.c6.text
Space: On the ISS, about 98% of water, including sweat and urine, is recycled into clean drinking water.

P.title: sp-astronauts.c7.text
Space: Spacewalks last six to eight hours. The suit is a mini spaceship with oxygen, cooling and pressure. Astronauts stay tethered at all times.

P.title: sp-astronauts.c8.text
Space: Many astronauts describe a shift in perspective after seeing Earth from space: a fragile blue ball with no visible borders.

P.title: sp-astronauts.c9.text
Space: After months in orbit, astronauts need weeks to readapt: balance is shaky, and things feel heavy. Some forget gravity and let go of objects mid-air.

P.title: sp-sky.summary
Space: Finding your way around the night sky.

P.title: sp-sky.q0.o1
Space: Use the Big Dipper's pointer stars

P.title: sp-sky.q1.q
Space: Which is brighter: magnitude 1 or magnitude 5?

P.title: sp-sky.c0.text
Space: Constellations are patterns of stars named by ancient cultures. Astronomers recognise 88 official ones. Their stars are usually not close to each other in space.

P.title: sp-sky.c0.viz.items.2.l
Space: stars visible on a dark night

P.title: sp-sky.c1.text
Space: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper's "bowl" upwards about five times their distance to reach Polaris, which barely moves and marks north.

P.title: sp-sky.c2.text
Space: Stars rise in the east and set in the west because Earth rotates. Long-exposure photos turn stars into circles around the celestial pole.

P.title: sp-sky.c3.text
Space: As Earth orbits the Sun, we see different constellations at night through the year. Orion rules winter evenings; Scorpius summer ones.

P.title: sp-sky.c4.text
Space: Orion is easy to find: three bright stars in a row form his belt. Red Betelgeuse marks a shoulder and blue Rigel a foot.

P.title: sp-sky.c5.text
Space: Astronomers measure brightness in magnitudes: lower numbers are brighter. Sirius, the brightest night star, is −1.5; the faintest naked-eye stars are about +6.

P.title: sp-sky.c6.text
Space: Planet comes from the Greek for "wanderer": planets move against the background stars over weeks, staying close to the Sun's path, the ecliptic.

P.title: sp-sky.c6.viz.steps.2
Space: A month later: moved against the stars

P.title: sp-sky.c7.text
Space: On a dark night, a pale band arches across the sky: the combined light of billions of stars in our galaxy's disc, seen edge-on from inside.

P.title: sp-sky.c8.text
Space: Your eyes need 20–30 minutes in darkness to fully adapt. Use a red light to read maps, because red barely disturbs night vision.

P.title: sp-sky.c8.viz.items.2
Space: Look slightly to the side of faint objects

P.title: sp-sky.c9.text
Space: Pick a moonless night, go away from lights, start with the Moon or a bright planet, then find Orion or the Big Dipper. Binoculars show far more than you'd expect.

P.title: sp-impacts.summary
Space: Space rocks and how we defend Earth.

P.title: sp-impacts.q0.q
Space: Which way do a comet's tails point?

P.title: sp-impacts.q0.x
Space: Pushed by sunlight and solar wind.

P.title: sp-impacts.q1.q
Space: What did NASA's DART mission show?

P.title: sp-impacts.q1.o1
Space: A spacecraft can change an asteroid's orbit

P.title: sp-impacts.c0.text
Space: Between Mars and Jupiter orbit millions of rocky bodies. Despite films, they're spread out: spacecraft cross the belt without dodging anything.

P.title: sp-impacts.c0.viz.items.0.w
Space: A crowded field of tumbling rocks

P.title: sp-impacts.c0.viz.items.0.r
Space: Mostly empty space, probes fly through safely

P.title: sp-impacts.c1.text
Space: Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt at about 940 km wide, is classed as a dwarf planet. NASA's Dawn found bright salt deposits on its surface.

P.title: sp-impacts.c2.text
Space: A comet is a "dirty snowball" of ice and dust a few km wide. Near the Sun, ice turns to gas, forming a glowing head and tails that always point away from the Sun.

P.title: sp-impacts.c2.viz.items.0
Space: Tails: point away from the Sun

P.title: sp-impacts.c2.viz.items.2
Space: Nucleus: icy core, a few km

P.title: sp-impacts.c3.text
Space: Edmond Halley predicted in 1705 that a comet seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 would return in 1758. It did, after his death. It next returns in 2061.

P.title: sp-impacts.c4.text
Space: Short-period comets come from the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune; long-period ones from the distant Oort Cloud, a shell perhaps a light-year away.

P.title: sp-impacts.c5.text
Space: About 66 million years ago, an asteroid around 10 km wide hit Mexico's Yucatán, making the Chicxulub crater. Dust and fires changed the climate and ended the non-bird dinosaurs.

P.title: sp-impacts.c6.text
Space: In 1908 an object exploded over Siberia, flattening about 80 million trees over 2,000 km². Nobody was killed because the area was so remote.

P.title: sp-impacts.c7.text
Space: In 2013 a 20-metre rock exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia. The shock wave shattered windows and injured about 1,500 people, mostly from flying glass.

P.title: sp-impacts.c8.text
Space: Telescopes track near-Earth asteroids. In 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into the moonlet Dimorphos and changed its orbit: the first test of deflecting an asteroid.

P.title: sp-impacts.c9.text
Space: Small rocks hit every day and burn up. Bigger impacts are rare: city-destroying ones about every few centuries, and dinosaur-killers every ~100 million years.

P.title: sp-dark.summary
Space: The 95% of the universe we can't see.

P.title: sp-dark.q0.q
Space: What fraction of the universe is ordinary matter?

P.title: sp-dark.q0.x
Space: The rest is dark matter and dark energy.

P.title: sp-dark.q1.q
Space: What is dark energy linked to?

P.title: sp-dark.q1.o1
Space: The accelerating expansion of the universe

P.title: sp-dark.c0.title
Space: What the universe is made of

P.title: sp-dark.c0.text
Space: Ordinary matter, everything made of atoms, is only about 5% of the universe. The rest is dark matter and dark energy, which we can't see directly.

P.title: sp-dark.c1.text
Space: In the 1970s Vera Rubin found that stars at galaxy edges orbit as fast as those near the centre. Visible matter alone couldn't hold them; something unseen adds gravity.

P.title: sp-dark.c2.text
Space: Back in 1933, Fritz Zwicky noticed galaxies in the Coma Cluster moved too fast to be held together by visible matter. He called the missing mass "dunkle Materie", dark matter.

P.title: sp-dark.c3.text
Space: When two galaxy clusters collided, the hot gas slowed down, but most of the mass, mapped by lensing, passed straight through: strong evidence for dark matter.

P.title: sp-dark.c4.text
Space: Dark matter doesn't emit or absorb light and barely interacts. Candidates include unknown particles like WIMPs or axions. Detectors deep underground have found nothing so far.

P.title: sp-dark.c5.text
Space: In 1998 two teams found that the universe's expansion is speeding up, not slowing. Something, called dark energy, pushes space apart. It won the 2011 Nobel Prize.

P.title: sp-dark.c6.text
Space: Type Ia supernovae all peak at about the same brightness, so how bright they look tells us how far away they are, like judging distance by a known light bulb.

P.title: sp-dark.c7.text
Space: On the largest scales, galaxies form a web of filaments and walls around huge empty voids, shaped by dark matter's gravity.

P.title: sp-dark.c8.text
Space: ESA's Euclid telescope, launched in 2023, is mapping billions of galaxies to measure how dark matter and dark energy shaped the universe.

P.title: sp-dark.c9.text
Space: Dark matter and dark energy are names for things we can measure but don't yet understand. Not knowing is where the most exciting science happens.

P.title: sp-satellites.q0.q
Space: How many satellites does GPS need for a position?

P.title: sp-satellites.q0.x
Space: The fourth fixes the clock error.

P.title: sp-satellites.q1.q
Space: Europe's satellite navigation system is called…

P.title: sp-satellites.c0.text
Space: Over 10,000 active satellites orbit Earth, most launched in the last few years for internet constellations. The first, Sputnik, launched in 1957.

P.title: sp-satellites.c1.text
Space: Satellites sit in different orbits for different jobs: low orbit for imaging and internet, medium for navigation, geostationary for TV and weather.

P.title: sp-satellites.c2.text
Space: Your phone receives time signals from at least four satellites. From the tiny differences in arrival time, it calculates its position to within a few metres.

P.title: sp-satellites.c3.text
Space: Three satellites fix your position in 3D; a fourth corrects your phone's cheap, imprecise clock. More satellites improve accuracy.

P.title: sp-satellites.c4.text
Space: Europe's own navigation system, Galileo, has over 25 satellites. Phones combine GPS (USA), Galileo (EU), GLONASS (Russia) and BeiDou (China).

P.title: sp-satellites.c5.text
Space: Geostationary satellites photograph the same half of Earth every few minutes, while polar orbiters scan the whole planet twice a day. Forecasts depend on both.

P.title: sp-satellites.c6.text
Space: Europe's Copernicus Sentinel satellites track wildfires, floods, crops, sea level and ice for free. Portuguese firefighters and farmers use the data.

P.title: sp-satellites.c7.text
Space: Over a million pieces of debris larger than 1 cm orbit Earth at bullet-like speeds. A collision can create thousands more fragments.

P.title: sp-satellites.c8.text
Space: Constellations of thousands of satellites in low orbit provide fast internet anywhere, including ships, planes and remote villages. Astronomers worry about streaks in their images.

P.title: sp-satellites.c9.text
Space: Portugal joined ESA in 2000, founded the Portugal Space agency in 2019 and launched its first satellite, the PoSAT-1 microsatellite, back in 1993.

P.title: sp-pioneers.summary
Space: How we learnt our place in the cosmos.

P.title: sp-pioneers.q1.q
Space: What did Kepler discover about orbits?

P.title: sp-pioneers.c0.text
Space: Babylonians recorded eclipses for centuries; Greeks measured the Earth. Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes estimated Earth's circumference using shadows in two cities.

P.title: sp-pioneers.c1.text
Space: Ptolemy's Earth-centred model, with planets moving on circles upon circles, predicted positions well enough to be used for 1,400 years.

P.title: sp-pioneers.c2.text
Space: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus published his Sun-centred model, moving Earth from the centre of the universe. It took a century to be widely accepted.

P.title: sp-pioneers.c3.text
Space: Tycho Brahe made the most precise naked-eye measurements ever. His assistant Johannes Kepler used them to discover that planets move in ellipses.

P.title: sp-pioneers.c4.text
Space: Galileo's support for a Sun-centred system led to his trial by the Inquisition in 1633. He spent his last years under house arrest.

P.title: sp-pioneers.c5.text
Space: In 1687 Newton's *Principia* explained Kepler's laws with universal gravitation and laws of motion: the same physics on Earth and in the heavens.

P.title: sp-pioneers.c5.viz.steps.2
Space: One law for apples and planets

P.title: sp-pioneers.c6.text
Space: William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781, the first planet found with a telescope. His sister Caroline Herschel discovered several comets.

P.title: sp-pioneers.c7.text
Space: In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that certain pulsing stars' periods reveal their true brightness, giving astronomers a cosmic measuring tape.

P.title: sp-pioneers.c7.viz.steps.2
Space: Compare with how bright it looks

P.title: sp-pioneers.c8.text
Space: In 1924 Edwin Hubble used Leavitt's method to show that Andromeda lies far outside the Milky Way. The universe suddenly contained countless galaxies.

P.title: sp-pioneers.c9.text
Space: Portuguese mathematician Pedro Nunes (1502–1578) improved navigation, studying rhumb lines and inventing the nonius, a scale for precise angle readings. A lunar crater bears his name.

P.title: sp-future.q0.q
Space: Why is the Moon's south pole attractive?

P.title: sp-future.q0.x
Space: Water for air, drinking and fuel.

P.title: sp-future.q1.q
Space: Which treaty forbids nations claiming the Moon?

P.title: sp-future.c0.text
Space: NASA's Artemis programme aims to return humans to the Moon for the first time since 1972 and build a long-term presence near the south pole.

P.title: sp-future.c0.viz.steps.1
Space: Artemis II: crew around the Moon

P.title: sp-future.c1.text
Space: Permanently shadowed craters there hold water ice, which could provide drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel.

P.title: sp-future.c2.text
Space: The Lunar Gateway is a planned small station orbiting the Moon, built by NASA, ESA, Japan and Canada, to support landings.

P.title: sp-future.c3.text
Space: Sending people to Mars needs huge rockets, radiation protection, life support for years and a way home. Most plans aim for the 2030s or later.

P.title: sp-future.c4.text
Space: Since 2021, private companies have flown paying tourists to the edge of space and to orbit. Tickets cost from hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of dollars.

P.title: sp-future.c5.text
Space: Some asteroids contain metals like nickel, iron and platinum. Mining them could supply future space industry, but it isn't economic yet.

P.title: sp-future.c6.text
Space: The nearest star is 4.2 light-years away; Voyager would take about 75,000 years. Ideas like tiny probes pushed by lasers might cut that to decades.

P.title: sp-future.c7.text
Space: Next-generation telescopes aim to photograph Earth-like exoplanets and analyse their air for signs of life, such as oxygen and methane together.

P.title: sp-future.c8.text
Space: The 1967 Outer Space Treaty says no nation can claim the Moon or planets, and space is free for all to explore peacefully. Resource mining is still debated.

P.title: sp-future.c9.text
Space: Space research gave us satellite navigation, weather forecasts, better medical imaging and water filters, and it answers the oldest question: are we alone?
